question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in ${\text{m/s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3+8t-3{t}^{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-1\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3+8t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3t+4{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3(0)+4(0)^{2}-(0)^{3}+C \\ -1 & =0+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3t+4{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}-1.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=2\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =3(2)+4(2)^{2}-(2)^{3}-1 \\  & =6+16-8-1 \\  & =13\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $13\,\text{m/s}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\sqrt{{t}^{3}},$ where $a(t)$ is measured in ${\text{m/s}}^{2}$ and $t$ is measured in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=1\,\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \sqrt{{t}^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{2}{5}(0)^{5/2}+C \\ 0 & =0+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=1\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}=\frac{2}{5}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{m/s}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{ft}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,\text{ft}/\text{s}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+C \\ 3 & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ 3 & =-2\cdot 0+C \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =3-2\cdot (-1) \\  & =5\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $5\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
question.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
question.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2}+2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{18{t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\sqrt{18{t}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-1,\,y={t}^{2}-t$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
question.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}-4t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,y={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{4}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The global extrema of a function are the lowest or highest points of the function's graph over its entire domain.

Which of the following statements are true with respect to the function $y=f(x)$ plotted above?

I. $f(x)$ has a stationary point at $x=-1$

II. $f(x)$ has a critical point at $x=-1$

III. $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=-1$
question.worked_solution:
Let's check our statements.

- Statement I is true. Stationary points are points where ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$ In this case, the graph of the function has a horizontal tangent line at $x=-1,$ and therefore, ${f}^{′}(-1)=0.$

- Statement II is true. The function has a critical point at $x=-1$ since each stationary point is a critical point.

- Statement III is false. The function has a local minimum at $x=-1$ since $f(-1)\le f(x)$ for all $x$ close enough to $x=-1.$

Therefore, statements I and II are true, while statement III is false.

question.knowledge_point: Dividing an Imaginary Number by a Complex Number
question.worked_solution:
The denominator is $2+\text{i}$ and its conjugate is $2-\text{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $2-\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{5\text{i}}{2+\text{i}} & =\frac{5\text{i}}{2+\text{i}}\cdot \frac{2-\text{i}}{2-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{10\text{i}-5{\text{i}}^{2}}{{2}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10\text{i}-5(-1)}{4-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{10\text{i}+5}{4+1} \\  & =\frac{5+10\text{i}}{5}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{5+10\text{i}}{5}=\frac{5}{5}+\frac{10}{5}\text{i}=1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: Second or Third Quadrant
question.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-8,-15).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$ Round your answer to two decimal places where necessary.
question.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+(-15)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64+225} \\  & =\sqrt{289} \\  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-15}{-8})| \\  & ≈1.080\,84.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the third quadrant, we add the reference angle to $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +1.080\,84 \\  & ≈4.22,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(17,4.22).$

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(17,4.22).$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{2x}-2x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
